rec-e-strahov-regiomontanus-ephemerides-1492
Status
Located · entry confidence A
Type
Printed Book
Subject
Astronomy (ephemerides)
Attested by
Straka 1913; Boldan 2025; Strahov Katalog Tritius; Munzar & Pařez 2002; Munzar 2001
Ownership marks
Inscription: fol. a2r: ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana’ (Straka 1913; Boldan 2025; Katalog Tritius 1064031). Later hands: ‘Ex libris Johannis Nachlovsky’ (fol. a1v) and ‘Nachlovsky’ (a2r) — later than Tycho per Boldan 2025; ‘Joannes Josephus Worell’ and ‘Anna’, with a drawn basket, on the second leaf (Straka 1913) Annotations: a 34-line Latin note on the winter of 1495/96 — deep snow, sledges over the roofs, the ‘Gallica scabies’ unknown before to Germans and Danes, an astrological reasoning from the planets in cold and wet signs, and a table of the seven planets' signs — on the verso of the leaf carrying December 1495 (‘fol. 75.b’ in the old foliation, Straka; ‘e4v’, Boldan 2025; ‘e14b (75v)’, Katalog Tritius), inside the 1492 almanac. Attributed to Tycho's own hand by Straka in 1913 on an undocumented comparison by eye; compared letter by letter, again by eye, with the DG IV 25 motto and the AG XI 56 dedication by Munzar & Pařez (2002), who find the hand ‘with a high probability’ Tycho's and at the least that of his immediate circle, and who date the winter to 1495/96 from independent climate records and a reconstruction of the planetary positions; called ‘vlastnoruční’ by Boldan (2025) — and called hypothetical by Pařez himself (2026). Never examined graphonomically. Binding: contemporary binding, bare wooden boards with a blind-tooled leather spine glued and brass-nailed (Straka 1913); ‘soudobá vazba’ covered in tanned leather with the blind-tooling now worn (Boldan 2025)
Surviving copy
DR VII 19/1–2 (old AG VII 84), Strahov Library (Strahovská knihovna, Královská kanonie premonstrátů na Strahově) · identification A · contemporary bare-board binding, not Tycho's bindery
fol. a2r: ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana’ (the Jesuit accession inscription; Straka 1913, Boldan 2025, Tritius); the 34-line weather note attributed to his hand (Straka 1913) — attribution open
No online catalogue record traced.
Dispersal
Channel VI, Clementinum leakage → Strahov (Strnad and the Mathematical Museum surplus, after 1773). Carries the 1642 inscription yet stands at Strahov. Straka 1913: Clementinum → the astronomer Antonín Strnad (d. 1799) → Strahov, whose purchase of Strnad's library is documented (Munzar 2001); Strahov's present cataloguer objects that the volume is in neither published catalogue of Strnad's library (Seydl 1939; Kouklová 1989) and suspects Straka confused it with Stoeffler–Pflaum's Almanach nova (Venice 1507), which did come from Strnad and bears AG VII 87. Boldan 2025 leaves it open whether Tycho acquired the volume before or after coming to Bohemia.
Later owners
Jesuit Clementinum 1642 → (Antonín Strnad, per Straka 1913 — disputed) → Strahov Library (old shelfmark AG VII 84; now DR VII 19/1–2)
Note
Not a second copy of Kleinschnitzová 14. Boldan 2025 (33.b, 33.c, 36.a): the National Library's Venice 1481 Ephemerides (his shelfmark 40 F 39; our Kleinschnitzová no. 14 records 14 H 188) LACKS its first gatherings a4 a10, and the Strahov volume CONTAINS exactly those gatherings, bound before the Augsburg 1492 Ephemerides 1492–1506 — the two are halves of one Tycho book, both inscribed by the Jesuits in 1642. Straka's ‘first incunable, Ephemerides c. 1476–82, a fragment lacking eight leaves and its end’ is the 1481 prefatory gatherings; his second, ‘Almanach … ad annos XV … 1492’, lacking seven leaves in the text and eighteen at the end, is the almanac that carries the note. The weather note is the case Pařez calls hypothetical; its attribution rests on Straka's eye and on content — the ‘Germanis et Danis’ of the plague sentence is the strongest internal pointer — and is recorded here as attributed, not as autograph.
Open questions
  • At the desk (18 September 2026): photograph the note whole and in overlapping details at pillar scale; establish which leaf carries it (quire signature and old foliation) and whether it is in the 1492 almanac as Boldan says; photograph the 1642 inscription, the Nachlovský and Worell hands, the spine (Mathematical-Museum red lines? Strnad's stamp?) and the boards.
  • Verify the National Library twin's current shelfmark (Boldan 2025: 40 F 39; Kleinschnitzová 14 / our record: 14 H 188) and that it indeed lacks gatherings a4 a10.
  • Obtain Munzar & Pařez 2002, pp. 360–375, and Voit 2015, nos. R-13/R-14.

Scaliger, Joseplt Justus: Opus novum de emendatione temporum ... Lutetiæ 1583.20. Kl. nr 41. – Prag, UB. – Detta är första upplagan av Scaligers stora verk. Tycho erhöll ett exemplar av Maior i Augsburg (brev från denne i juni 1584; VII, 83) 1 ett annat från Brucæus i Rostock vid samma tid (VII, 86). Scaliger, Joseph ]ustus: Opus de emendatione temporum: castigatius et multis partibus auctius ... Lugduni Batav. 1598. 2°. Braunsberg, Bibliothek der Staatlichen Akademie. Originalbd med porträtt och vapen. I sept. 1595 (VII, 373) skriver Tycho till Pontanus, som då befann sig i Holland, att han önskade, att denne skulle sända Scaligers »de Emendatione Temporum præstans illud opus recognitum, ubi illud consummatum fuerit» – varmed tydligen menas föreliggande upplaga, som då ännu icke förelåg färdigtryckt. Måhända var det Pontanus, som sedan skickade det exemplar som nu finns i Braunsberg. Tycho måste ha fått verket kort efter dess publicering. Förordet är nämligen dat. d. 11 jan. 1598 (g.st.) och i mars s.å. (VIII, 32) tackar han Scaliger för dennes omnämnande av honom i boken, som han fått »just i dagarna». Tycho syftar på den tabell över sina observationer av ekvinoktierna som Scaliger på ett smickrande sätt meddelat på s. 728-729: »Tabella requinoctii utriusque in Dania observati ab eximio artifice nobiliss. Tychone Brahe.» Denna tabell är den som Tycho tryckte i »Prog.» (Il, 15) och som han måste ha skickat Scaliger tidigare, väl genom samme Pontanus, som i ett odaterat brev, sannolikt från slutet av 1597 eller början av 1598 (VIII, 20), omtalar, att Scaliger satt in Tychos observationer i verket och att Tycho snart skall få se dem. Dreyer menar i en not (»Tycho Brahe», s. 270, 1 efter Kästner, »Geschichte der Mathematik», 2, Gött. 1797, s. 409), att Scaliger som tack för några böcker Tycho skickat honom sänt honom ett exemplar av sina »Conjecturæ et notæ in Varronem», vilket exemplar Tycho skänkte eller lånade professor Taubmann i Wittenberg. Denna notis grundar sig på en fullständig missuppfattning av ett ställe i Taubmanns kommentar till Plautus »Pcenulus», vers 34 ff. (M. Acci Plauti »Comœdiæ XX. superstites ... ». Wittebergæ 16121 s. 309). Taubmann hänvisar här dels till Scaligers »Conject. Varron.», dels till sammes »in Appendice operis, De emendatione temporum». Längre ned refereras till Scaliger »in Emendata quidem prædicti Operis editione». Detta syftar givetvis icke på hans »Conject. Varron.» – som Kästner och efter honom Dreyer trott – utan på den strax förut nämnda »De emendatione temporum». Vi kunna också fastställa, att upplagan 1598 avses. Endast i denna och ej i någon annan upplaga står det av Taubmann citerade stället i ett appendix, »In Fragmentum Berosi Babylonii», s. XXV. Vidare berättar Taubmann i sin Plautus-kommentar, att Scaliger skickat Tycho boken, som just lämnat pressen. Tycho var då i Wittenberg, skriver Taubmann. Det var vid ung. samma tid som han skänkte Taubmann ett exemplar av sin »Mech.» (Berlin-exemplaret) och Taubmann å sin sida sjöng hans lov i ett alkaiskt ode till kejsar Rudolf (dat. d. 21 okt. 1598; avskrift bl.a. i slutet på ett exemplar av Resen, »Inscriptiones Haffnienses», Det kgl. Bibliotek, Köpenhamn) . Dreyer har varit tveksam om Tycho skänkte eller lånade Taubmann sitt exemplar (det står concessit hos Taubmann). Att det varit fråga om ett lån, framgår dock av vad Taubmann själv skriver om detta exemplar i ett brev till Scaliger, sannolikt från våren 1599 (i: P. Burmannus' »Sylloge epistolarum a vi ris illustribus scriptarum», T . 2, Leidæ 1727, s. 339): »quem hisce diebus ab amicissimo et pome mihi domestico, Tychone Brahe utendum habui». Taubmanns uppgift i Plautus-kommentaren är emellertid icke fullt klar. Ty det exemplar av verket varom Tycho talar i brevet till Scaliger i mars 1598 var säkerligen icke något gåvoexemplar från denne. Hade så varit fallet, skulle Tycho omtalat det som en gåva och framfört sitt tack därför, vilket han icke gör – utan han tackar Scaliger för dennes omnämnande av hans observationer. Och vidare befann sig Tycho då på Wandsbek, icke i W ittenberg. Inget tyder på, att detta exemplar varit en skänk från Scaliger. Däremot synes Tycho, om vi få tro Taubmann, ha erhållit ett dedikationsexemplar från Scaliger under vistelsen i Wittenberg, vilket exemplar dock icke var så färskt som Taubmann skriver. Sca/iger, Julius Ccesar: De causis linguæ latinæ libri XIII. [Heidelbergæ] 1584.80. Pr. nr 52. Kl. nr 8: r. – Prag, UB. I ett saml.-bd. Originalbd med porträtt och vapen.

Kleinschnitzová 1933 no.17; NK Clementinum Sign. 14 J 164. Kleinschnitzová's verdict: 'Kein Tychonianum' — the volume's lead work (Scheiner, Pantographice seu Ars delineandi) is not from Tycho's library; ownership rejected. The ground is the imprint: the Pantographice was printed at Rome in 1631, thirty years after Tycho's death. The volume itself is genuinely his — it is built round Christmann's Observationum solarium libri tres (Basel, 1601), which carries 'Ex Bibliotheca Tijchoniana' and the autograph 'Emi Pragae mense Majo' — but the Jesuits bound the Scheiner in ahead of it, and it leads the volume only by accident of rebinding.

Thaddaeus Hagecius (Hájek), Dialexis de novae et prius incognitae stellae ... apparitione. Francofurti ad Mcenum, 1574

rec-e-norlind-hagecius-dialexis
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Type
Printed Book
Subject
Astronomy (nova 1572)
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hagecius, Thaddceus)
Acquisition
received/gift (author-corrected copy) (Author / correspondent gift)
Ownership marks
Annotations: Hagecius's autograph corrections & additions
Note
Norlind 1970: "Måste Tycho ha ägt" (Tycho must have owned it), cf. Progymnasmata III,19-43, where the Dialexis is treated in detail — the strongest of the four Hagecius attestations, and the only one in which Norlind uses an explicit ownership verb. Dreyer 1890 + Mosley 2007 (Bearing the Heavens, 'Books and the heavens') document that Hagecius sent Tycho a copy carrying many manuscript corrections and additions in his own hand, hoping Tycho would reprint it; Tycho instead discussed the revised text in the Progymnasmata. So Tycho owned a specific, author-corrected copy: the most identifiable of the missing Hagecius copies, since it would carry Hagecius's autograph corrections as well as, probably, a Tycho ownership mark. It is unlocated, and it completes a striking gap — Tycho owned at least four works by Hagecius, yet not one survives in any of the four inventories (Prandtl, Kleinschnitzová, Šolc, Mortensen). Two copies of the Frankfurt 1574 edition are held by the Czech National Library — one inscribed for the Jesuit College at Chomutov ('Collegij Soctis IESV Commotonij Ao. 1671', doc 000154680), one stamped for the Prague academic library ('REGIAE BIBLIOTH: ACAD: PRAGEN.', doc 000014579) — but the copy-level provenance notes in both catalogue records show only those later owners. No Tycho mark is recorded in either, neither copy has been examined in person, and no Hajek-autograph copy has surfaced.
Norlind 1970, p. 349

Theodor Zwinger (comp.), Theatri humanae vitae Volumen decimum-octavum [vol. XVIII]. Basel Basel, 1587

rec-e-prandtlA-57
Status
Located · entry confidence A
Type
Printed Book
Subject
Encyclopaedia/commonplace (humanae vitae)
Attested by
Prandtl 1932, Verz. A no. 57 (Verz. B, Band XXV); Mortensen 1955, pp. 29-30 (Röhsska, ex Per Hierta); Supralibros note
Ownership marks
Inscription: Gilt superexlibris — Tycho's portrait (upper board) and arms (lower board), each in an oval medallion ringed by a Latin distich ('Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat quae latet interior' and 'Arma genus fundi pereunt, durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent'). Binding: A typical Renaissance trade binding — brown leather over boards, blind-tooled roll-borders and corner stamps, metal clasps — which Tycho acquired already bound and then stamped with his gilt portrait+arms superexlibris (Mortensen 1965, pp. 29-30). Not a purpose-made Uraniborg presentation Prachtband: the splendour is the applied gilt mark, not the binding itself. The superexlibris is especially finely struck and well preserved — the exemplar reproduced (press-gilt) on the cover of Lauritz Nielsen, Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri (1946), and figured in Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde X (1906/07).
Surviving copy
(inventory number not recorded), Röhsska Museum · identification A
Tycho's gilt portrait+arms superexlibris — the finely struck, well-preserved exemplar reproduced (press-gilt) on the cover of Lauritz Nielsen, Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri (1946), and figured in Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde X (1906/07). On a Renaissance trade binding Tycho acquired already bound.
No online catalogue record traced.
Bound with: (unidentified — a gilt-supralibros Prachtband), A Tycho gilt-supralibros Prachtband (title not identified)
Dispersal
Channel II, Heirs' sale / dispersal (post-1601). Dispersed from Tycho's library after 1601; the route to Sweden is undocumented (possibly the 1648 Swedish sack of Prague — channel III — but unconfirmed). By the early 20th c. in the collection of Baron Per Hierta (1864–1924) of Frammestad, Sweden; now at the Röhsska Konstslöjdmuseum, Göteborg. The route INTO Röhsska is unresolved: either Hjalmar Wijk's 1915 donation of Hierta books to the museum, or the posthumous Björck & Börjesson auction (Stockholm, Oct-Nov 1932, cat. 272, 1618 lots) that dispersed the rest of Hierta's collection.
Later owners
Baron Per Hierta (1864–1924), Frammestad, Sweden → Röhsska Konstslöjdmuseum, Göteborg
Note
Theatri humanae vitae vol. XVIII (Basel 1587), Theodor Zwinger's great Basel encyclopaedia — a mighty folio Tycho acquired already bound and stamped with his gilt portrait+arms superexlibris. Prandtl 1932 catalogued it as no.57 / Einzelband XXV; Mortensen 1965 (pp. 29-30) identifies that same volume as the one 'now in the Röhsska Konstslöjdmuseum, Göteborg; formerly Per Hierta, Frammestad'. Its superexlibris is the exemplar reproduced on the binding of Lauritz Nielsen's Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri (1946). One of the few Tychonica that reached Nordic rather than Prague/Clementinum hands.
Open questions
  • Resolve the acquisition route into Röhsska — Hjalmar Wijk's 1915 donation of Hierta books vs the 1932 Björck & Börjesson posthumous sale (cat. 272) — via the museum's accession register (year of accession).

rec-e-mort-kb-fincke
Status
Disputed · entry confidence C
Type
Printed Book
Subject
Mathematics/Geometry
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 345 (s.v. Fincke, Thomas)
Ownership marks
Inscription: No Tycho mark on either KB copy (both examined on their surrogates). The Geometria rotundi is dedicated to King Frederik II; in the dedication Fincke praises 'in Mathematis excellentissimum virum Dn. Tychonem Brahe' (printed text, present in every copy) — this is Norlind's whole basis, not a copy-level Tycho mark.
Surviving copies
LN 599 4 ex.1 (Royal Library, Copenhagen), Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek) examined and ruled out · identification D
No Tycho mark. Title-page autograph 'Horrebow'; royal crowned cipher + BIBLIOTHECA REGIA HAFNIENSIS stamp; 18th-c marbled-board binding.
Links: digital facsimile (Early European Books)
Hielmst. 1661a 4 (= LN 599 4 ex.2; sammelband with Ursus, Fundamentum astronomicum, Strasbourg 1588), Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek) examined and ruled out · identification D
No Tycho mark. Contemporary limp-vellum sammelband (gothic-MS pastedown). Flyleaf: 'Severinus Pauli[?]... Lipsiae Anno Dni 158[3]' + mottoes 'Superna curato, Humana contemnito' / 'Mens generosa ultra polos'. Title page: 'Christiernus Joannis Hafniensis Anno 1620' + motto 'Ex uno omnia'. Hielmstierne bookplate No.1661 + BRH stamp.
Links: digital facsimile (Early European Books)
Note
Thomas Fincke, Geometriae rotundi libri XIIII (Basel: S. Henricpetri, 1583), the major Danish trigonometry/geometry treatise, dedicated to Frederik II. Both KB copies have been examined through the EEB surrogates, and neither bears any Tycho ownership mark. Copy 1 (LN 599 4 ex.1): autograph 'Horrebow' (the 18th-c Danish Royal Astronomer family) on the title page + royal-cipher/BRH stamps; 18th-c marbled-board binding. Copy 2 (Hielmst. 1661a 4 / ex.2): a contemporary sammelband (Fincke 1583 + Ursus, Fundamentum astronomicum, Strasbourg 1588) in limp vellum, inscribed 'Severinus Pauli[?]... Lipsiae Anno Dni 158[3]' (mottoes 'Superna curato, Humana contemnito' / 'Mens generosa ultra polos') and 'Christiernus Joannis Hafniensis Anno 1620' (motto 'Ex uno omnia'), later Hielmstierne. Norlind nonetheless placed the book in Tycho's library — 'fanns säkerligen i biblioteket på Uraniborg' (Bilaga I, p. 345) — but his whole basis is Fincke's printed praise of Tycho in the preface, a compliment present in every copy rather than a mark in any copy. No inventory, inscription or ownership mark attests Tycho's ownership, and neither surviving KB copy is his. No published census lists this work.
Norlind 1970, p. 345
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Fincke, Thomas: Geometriæ rotundi libri XIIII. Basileæ 1583. 4°. Fincke bedrev studier vid olika utländska universitet, bl.a. i Basel 1583, blev vid 30 års ålder professor i matematik i Köpenhamn 1591, i retorik 1602 och i medicin 1603. Erhöll 1597 uppdraget att jämte professor Iver Stub resa över till Hven för att undersöka om någon åverkan gjorts på Tychos instrument, vilket misstänkliggjorde dem i Tychos ögon. – Boken är tillägnad konung Fredrik II, men i förordet till läsaren, fol. 3r, talar Fincke mycket vänligt om Tycho och ber honom inte dölja, om det finns något lovvärt i den och icke spara kritik, om så behövs. Boken, som tillkommit under Finckes studievistelse i Basel, fanns säkerligen i biblioteket på Uraniborg.
Open questions
  • Identify the two early owners of copy 2 (Severinus Pauli[?], Leipzig c.1583; Christiern Jensen of Copenhagen, 1620); neither is Tycho.

The National Library catalogues the volume as 14 B 38: Witelo, Nuremberg: Petreius 1535, with Dürer's Latin Institutiones geometricae (four books), Paris: Wechel 1532, bound in as the first adligatum; Šolc 2002 prints XIV B 38, 1585 and 1582. The catalogue's provenance note names the Jesuit college (1636) and the Mathematical Museum and records no Tycho note, so the identification rests on Šolc's reading of the initials and the verse annotations. Dispersal

Later owners
Jesuit Clementinum 1642
Note
Kleinschnitzová 1933 no.6; NK Clementinum Sign. 5 G 42. A composite volume of five works, three of which Kleinschnitzová marks «Kein Tychonianum» — the Aristarchus (1572), the Maestlin, and de Buckaw's Problema mathematicum of 1641, printed forty years after Tycho died. The volume itself is his. She records the Jesuit accession inscription on the title-page of the third work, Heron's Spiritalium liber (Urbino 1575): «Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae A° 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tijchonis»; and of the fifth, Werner's Libellus super vigintiduobus elementis conicis (Nuremberg 1522), that it «hat Marginalien von Brahes Hand» and is probably the copy Norlind lists as his no. 32. The Prague catalogue says the same of the volume: that it comes from Tycho Brahe's library and carries his marginalia. It is bound in the white leather of the Clementinum Jesuit college — one of the volumes Kleinschnitzová cites to show that Tycho's Sammelbände were broken up after 1642 and rebound with books of other provenance, which is how three works that were never his came to sit inside one that was.

4Surviving volumes

The 71 physical volumes identified as Tycho’s own, holding 114 of the catalogued works, arranged by holding institution. Each volume is given with its present shelfmark, the earlier catalogue numbers, the marks that secure its identification and their grade, its bound-in contents, the verbatim copy-level provenance note of the holding library where one is published, and direct links to the catalogue record of every bound-in constituent and to the digital facsimile where one exists. The 2 volumes marked Tychoniana but not his and the 3 copies examined and ruled out follow in sections of their own.

For the Prague volumes the National Library’s own catalogue record, as published in Manuscriptorium, is quoted beneath the constituents: the binding and physical description, the former owners with the dates the catalogue attaches, provenance notes not already given, the library’s notes on each tract, the literature the record cites, and the digital copy where one exists — in the library’s Czech, verbatim. Where the printed manuscript catalogue has been retro-converted, its entry is quoted too.

Ze zavazování na dvě dvojice zelených tkanic dochován jen fragment jedné na zadní desce.
Physical description, as catalogued
Kodex, kniha, rukopis. · 19 + I ff. 22 cm × 15 cm · Pergamen. · Condition: Rukopis mírně poškozen zašpiněním. · Hand: Snad jde o autograf Tychona Brahe.
Contents, as catalogued
Tabulae sinuum Švédsko, Ven (Hven) (?) (V době, kdy rukopis vznikl, náležel ostrov Hven Dánsku.), 1582 ?
  1. Přední přídeští-1r — Vlastnické záznamy a signatury, kromě toho na f. 1r rukou Tychona Brahe řecký zápis. — Greek
  2. 1v-19r — Tycho (Tyge Ottesen) Brahe — Tabulae sinuum — Dříve vypočítané tabulky, které Tycho Brahe převzal a opravil.
Origin, as catalogued
Švédsko, Ven (Hven) (?), 1582 ? Podle literatury jde o autograf Tychona Brahe, a pak vznikl nejspíše v jeho observatoři na ostrově Ven (Hven). (V době, kdy byl rukopis napsán, náležel ostrov Hven Dánsku.) Tycho Brahe jako majitel kodexu je dosvědčen iniciálami na přední desce a zápisem na f. 1r.
Provenance, as catalogued
Na zadní desce papírový štítek se signaturou Tres. M 1. Na předním přídeští starší signatury Tres. M 1, TB/LI cim. 52 (? - písmeno L vyškrabáno) a současné signatury VI.E.9 (razítkem na štítku) a Cim D 82. Na f. 1r rukou vlastnický záznam jezuitské koleje u sv. Klimenta na Starém Městě pražském Collegii Caesarei Societatis Iesu Pragae anno 1642. Ex bibliotheca Tichoniana a současná signatura VI.E.9. Na f. Iv rukopisný záznam Numerorum scientia (patrně stejný záznam ještě jednou rozmazán).

Sign. VII E 29 — National Library of the Czech Republic (Clementinum)

Earlier catalogues
Prandtl, Verz. B, Band IV; Kleinschnitzová no. 24
Identification
A · identified by Kleinschnitzová 1933 (FK-24) / Prandtl Verzeichnis A no.41
Marks securing the identification
Tychoniana provenance per Kleinschnitzová 1933 (FK-24) and Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 41. Prandtl calls it a copy in Tycho's own hand; that attribution has not been checked against the dating of the codex.
Contents
  1. Sacrobosco, Joannes de, Sphaera Johannis de Sacrobusto in compendium digesta (1539) (no. 176)
Manuscriptorium
VII.E.29 (manuscript description) · VII. E. 29. (entry of the printed catalogue, retro-converted) · digital copy (73 images) — the library’s record as of 17 April 2026
Binding, as described by the library
Lepenkové desky potažené papírem a přes hřbet a na rozích desek kůží. Na hřbetě zlacené linky a titul Johannis de Sacro Sphaera. Vpředu i vzadu jedna papírová předsádka, stejným papírem jsou vylepena i přídeští.
Physical description, as catalogued
Kodex, kniha, rukopis. · II + 31 + I ff. 20,5 cm × 15 cm · Papír.
Contents, as catalogued
Commentum in Johannis de Sacrobosco tractatum de sphaera Německo (Norimberk?), první polovina 16. století (nejdříve 1539), podle dalších děl obsažených v původním konvolutu snad začátek 40. let
  1. Ir-Iv — Vlastnický záznam, údaje o obsahu dřívějšího konvolutu, astronomický nákres, zkoušky pera a další poznámky. — la
  2. 1r-31r — Commentum in Johannis de Sacrobosco tractatum de sphaera — Podle úvodní rubriky (s letopočtem 1539), závěru a zpracování 4. knihy je patrně velmi příbuzný text dochován v rukopisu Universitätsbibliothek München 4o Cod. Ms. 746, f. 1r-21r. — la
Origin, as catalogued
Německo (Norimberk?), první polovina 16. století (nejdříve 1539), podle dalších děl obsažených v původním konvolutu snad začátek 40. let.
Provenance, as catalogued
Na f. Ir jméno dřívějšího majitele, norimberského astronoma Andrease Schönera a zapsané ceny původních částí konvolutu a cena za svázání s celkovým součtem (vzhledem k datům vydání tištěných částí konvolutu a Schönerovu roku narození 1528 je jeho vlastnický záznam snad mladší). Na f. Ir a 1r (zde dvakrát) iniciály pozdějšího majitele Tychona Brahe T B. Na f. 31v signatura O VII 44 (upravovaná vyškrabáváním a přepisováním). Na f. Ir dále tužkou údaj o starším umístění v konvolutu Antea praeligatum tractatui Lucae Gaurici Norimbergae a. 1540 edito, sign. 14.F.16., Truhlářův katalog uvádí další obsah konvolutu Albubatris Genethliacus, Norimbergae 1540, Hieronymi Cardani libelli duo, Norimbergae 1543.
Ve spodní části hřbetu štítek s částí současné signatury (29). Na přední desce štítek s dřívější pomocnou signaturou Tres. M 24, která se opakuje i na předním přídeští. Tam také přírůstkové číslo (?) A. B. 5/1900, údaj T B. 6 (číslo 6 přepsáno na 24) a současná signatura MS VII E 29.
Entry of the printed catalogue (retro-converted; record)
Sphaera in compendium digesta. Anno salutis nostre . a. 1539 Secundum notas folio praeligato inscriptas codex hic una cum libris impressis olim adligatis (Lucae Gaurici Tractatus astrologiae iudiciariae, Norimb.
ff. 31, 20,5 x 15,5 cm. chart.

No Tycho autograph mark. The dense annotations are Paul Wittich's, not Tycho's -- Gingerich (Census, pp. 105-108) retracts the earlier Tycho-annotation belief, noting the flyleaf longitude list cites Vratislavia (Wittich's Wrocław) but neither Hven nor Copenhagen. Tycho ownership rests on Gingerich's documented acquisition history (one of the copies Monau brought to Prague for Tycho in Oct 1600 -- Gingerich, Census, pp. 105-108; Mosley p. 179 puts the number despatched at three), not on a Tycho mark.

Richly annotated by Wittich (4 prelim. pp. + 30 pp. after f.196); observation notes incl. a Venus-Regulus conjunction 16 Sept 1574 and a Jupiter-Fomalhaut conjunction 8 Nov 1572. Later owners
Antiquariat Weiss & Co., Munich (by 1932) → sold to America → Oscar Ekman, engineer, and Lia Ekman, Copenhagen → their gift to the Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg, 1957 (inventory 1957:0030) → deposited by the museum at the Royal Library, Copenhagen, manuscript department (Björklund 1992)
Sources
Prandtl 1932; Norlind 1970; Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957; Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart); Björklund 1992; Grinder-Hansen 2006; Gingerich 2002
Notes
Prandtl’s Band II, the student binding of 1561. Prandtl recorded it in 1932 at Antiquariat Weiss & Co., Munich, and as sold to America; Gingerich (2002) still placed it at an undisclosed location, and this reconstruction carried it as a private, untraced volume until September 2026. It had in fact returned to Denmark within a generation: the Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg reported it among the acquisitions of 1956–57 as the gift of Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman, and Norlind placed it there in 1970. The museum’s register, inventory 1957:0030, describes the binding, the inscriptions, Tycho’s added latitudes for Helsingborg, Lund and Visby on fol. 53 of the Apianus, and a restoration by Birgitte Dall in 1957; its two photographs show the front board and the purchase note. Björklund (1992) reported the volume deposited at the Royal Library’s manuscript department, and the Nationalmuseet catalogue of 2006 reproduced it from a Royal Library photograph. Present custody, Royal Library deposit or museum store, is to be confirmed with both institutions.

Notes of the library
Číslo jednotky: __AG VII 84 = DR VII 19
Jedno z vydání kumulovaných hvězdářských tabulek, které započaly vycházet v autorově tiskárně už roku 1474.
Premonstráti (Strahov) |AG VII 84 = DR VII 19
Na fol. 1a1b záznam z konce 16. století "Ex libris Johanni Nachlovskij" a na fol. 1a2a "Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana". O Tychonově vlastnictví (1546 - 1601) svědčí autografní zápis meteorologické povahy na fol. e14b (75v) druhého přívazku. Pak se konvolut stal součástí tzv. Matematického muzea v Klementinu, odkud přešel na Strahov (původní signatura AG VII 84). Cyril Straka: Zápis Tychona Brahe v knihovně Strahovské. Časopis Českého muzea 87, 1913, s. 382-384, zvl. 384 uvádí, že konvolut přešel na Strahov počátkem 19. století jakožto součást knihovny astronoma Antonína Strnada (1746 - 1799). To&nbsp;se však nezdá být pravděpodobné, neboť Seydl&nbsp;ani Kouklová&nbsp;v katalogu&nbsp;Strnadovy knihovny tuto položku neuvádějí. Je možné, že u Straky došlo k záměně s&nbsp;efemeridami, které sestavili Johann Stoeffler - Jakob Pflaum: Almanach nova plurimis annis&nbsp;[1499 - 1531] venturis inservientia. Venezia, Peter Liechtenstein 1507 (EDIT 16 CNCE 35579), v nichž se nachází Regiomontanova předmluva. Tyto efemeridy&nbsp;se do Strahovské knihovny&nbsp;dostaly skutečně ze Strnadova majetku a nesou signaturu AG VII 87 (srov. Kouklová, s. 217, č. 459, kde však záznam veden mylně jako prvotisk s odvoláním na H 15085, což je předchozí edice z Ulmu 1499).&nbsp;
Chybí 358 listů. Dochována je&nbsp;jen&nbsp;složka 1a4 s Ratdoltovou a Regiomontanovou předmluvou a ze&nbsp;složky 2a pouze fol. a5-6 Mariensüssova Expositia. ; Natištěné iniciály v červeno-černém tisku nekolorovány, rubriky nedoplněny. Před hlavním dílem předvázány [3] zachovalé předsádkové listy s matematickými výpočty, sahajícími až na nepotištěné fol. 1a1a, kde se jejich autor ca 1766 nad kresbičkou koše podepsal "Josephus Worel". Táž ruka nesoustavně pročíslovala listy celého konvolutu.
Hlavní dílo konvolutu v pozdně gotické vazbě na prkénkových deskách 230 x 150 potažených usní jen do jedné třetiny (přední deska mírně naprasklá). Přídeštní část usně, přibitá k deskám malými hřebíčky, byla zdobena dnes už zcela setřelým slepotiskem s rámovou kompozicí. U horního kapitálu poškozený hřbet nebyl zdoben. (private; no shelfmark) — Private / untraced (the American collectors of the Gemma, via Martayan Lan 2001, and of the ‘T.B.O. 1583’ Apianus; formerly Antiquariat Weiß & Co., Munich)

Identification
A · identified by Harald Mortensen 1955, p. 30 (from Felix Mainx's report of 1938); Norlind 1970, p. 347; the annotations recognised as Tycho's by Owen Gingerich (per litteras, 25 May 2001) and Anthony Grafton (report for Martayan Lan, 2001); Gingerich 2002, p. 326
Marks securing the identification
Tycho's autograph annotations throughout, from a word or two to a note filling the margin, incl. the long note written upside down in the lower margin of Book II, pp. 124–125 (the hand confirmed by Owen Gingerich, per litteras 25 May 2001, and studied by Anthony Grafton); Tycho's gilt portrait supralibros with the motto ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior’ on the front cover and the Brahe arms with ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’ on the back
Binding
contemporary flexible vellum with yapp edges, the portrait-and-arms supralibros (Martayan Lan 2001)
Contents
  1. Cornelius Gemma, De naturae divinis characterismis; seu raris & admirandis spectaculis, causis, indiciis, proprietatibus rerum in partibus singulis universi, libri II (Antwerp, Christopher Plantin, 1575) (1575) (no. 44)
Links
No online catalogue record traced; the location rests on the source named above.
Later owners
Felix Mainx, Prague (acquired 1938; he told Harald Mortensen of it, and Mortensen printed the fact in Fund og Forskning 2, 1955, p. 30) → ‘a private European collector’ (Martayan Lan's provenance line, 2001) → Martayan Lan, New York, Catalogue 28 (2001), item 55, offered at US$ 300,000 → a private American collector (Gingerich 2002, p. 326 n. 16)
Sources
Martayan Lan Cat. 28 (2001); Gingerich 2002; Mortensen 1955; Norlind 1970
Notes
Martayan Lan's description (Catalogue 28, item 55, pp. 66–67, headed ‘Tycho Brahe reads & annotates the new star of 1572: unpublished notes on “the greatest cosmological crisis in Western history” – Grafton’): 4to; 229, (1) pp., (5) ff., 284 pp., 18 ff.; three woodcut star charts and several depictions of constellations and related astronomical phenomena in the text. Binding: contemporary flexible vellum with yapp edges, gilt medallion portrait of Tycho in the centre of the front cover, worn, ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior’ in the surround; the back cover with the Brahe family arms and ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’; covers soiled, remnants of ties; an old shelfmark stencilled on the spine. Condition: front endleaf soiled, with unidentified later annotations; waterstain and soiling in the upper right corner of the title and scattered leaves; a scored former ownership inscription and a later inscription dated 1647; even toning, occasional light browning; ‘for a working copy, very good’. Price US$ 300,000. The annotations in Tycho's hand range from a word or two to virtually filling the margin; on pp. 124–25 of Book II the lower-margin note was entered with the copy held upside down (the colour plate at the front of the catalogue, captioned ‘Tycho Brahe's Annotated Copy No. 55’; Gingerich 2002, fig. 1). The dealer supplied a list of the annotated locations with a partial transcription, and Anthony Grafton's detailed but preliminary report, available on request, which found a genetic relation to the Progymnasmata (Prague 1602); Owen Gingerich confirmed the hand (per litteras 25 May 2001) and wrote that the book ‘contains source material used directly by Tycho in composing his Progymnasmata … this is a working text that is feeding directly into his published work, and we have nothing else like this’. Called by the dealer ‘one of only two known copies of any book owned by the astronomer in private hands’. Provenance as given: ‘a private European collector. In 1955, the Danish librarian H. Mortensen described the present copy as being in the private collection of a professor in Prague’ – that is Felix Mainx, who told Mortensen in 1938 that he had acquired Tycho's copy (Mortensen 1955, p. 30, read verbatim); Gingerich 2002, p. 326, which has the book in Mortensen's own collection about 1955, misreads the paper. Gingerich 2002, p. 327: Tycho annotated heavily the section on Muñoz's observations of the new star of 1572 and quoted the passage in the Progymnasmata; n. 16: now in the hands of a private American collector. References cited by the dealer: Norlind 1970, p. 347; Adams G-373; Durling 2042; Warner, The Sky Explored, p. 92; Daston & Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, p. 175; Christianson 2000, p. 139; Prandtl 1932 (cited by the offprint pagination, pp. 1–16).

Links
No online catalogue record traced; the location rests on the source named above.
Later owners
a monastery library in the Low Countries, until about 1960 (the star names written in French on the planisphere and a note partly in Dutch, partly in Flemish on the facing page place the volume around Antwerp or Brussels for a very long time) → a private owner in Belgium, who wrote to Gingerich about 2000 → an anonymous American collector, ‘who must have paid close to a million dollars for it’ (Gingerich 2002, p. 328)
Sources
Gingerich 2002
Notes
Gingerich 2002, pp. 327–328: about two years before he wrote (so about 2000) an e-mail enquiry came from Belgium about a copy of Apianus's Astronomicum Caesareum bound with an even rarer equatorium, an earlier one by Johann Schöner: why, the owner asked, would books printed in 1521 and 1540 be in a binding stamped 1583, with the initials TBO above the date? Gingerich recognised Tycho's mark at once. Further enquiries showed several annotations by Tycho, all in the comet section near the end; fig. 2 (‘courtesy of another private collector’) is a detail of f. O1 verso with Tycho's marginalia beside the table of the comet's daily motion. Additional early annotations in other hands – the star names on the planisphere in French, a note on the facing page partly Dutch and partly Flemish – place the book around Antwerp or Brussels for a very long time; until about 1960 it was in a monastery library. Gingerich imagines it migrated to the Low Countries by the same Jesuit hands that brought the Wittich Copernicus to Liège. ‘This extraordinary volume has changed hands again, to an anonymous American collector who must have paid close to a million dollars for it.’ Gingerich, who had examined over a hundred copies of the Astronomicum Caesareum without finding one associated with Tycho, took this to be the copy Tycho retained when he gave Wittich his (the Chicago copy, with Tycho's presentation inscription; Tycho later complained it had cost him 20 florins). It is distinct from both the Chicago copy and the copy Tycho inscribed at Wittenberg on 14 June 1599, now at Gotha (Prandtl Band VI). Neither the monastery, the Belgian owner nor the American buyer is named.

Annotation census

Annotation census. 28 of the digitised volumes have been surveyed page by page for manuscript additions: 12,830 pages examined, 992 of them carrying handwriting of some kind. The survey locates writing and classifies it by kind (marginal notes, underlining, corrections, ownership inscriptions, stamps); it does not attribute a hand. The Prague volumes carry, besides whatever Tycho wrote, the hands of earlier owners and the Jesuits’ accession notes of 1642. The page numbers are given so that the facsimile can be consulted directly; no reading of the annotations is offered here.

7The ownership marks

Tycho’s books are recognised by the marks his own bindery and his own hand put on them. The bindery on Hven produced a datable sequence: name-stamps in the student years, the gilt cipher T.B.O. (Tychonis Brahe Ottonidis) on brown calf from about 1565, the same cipher with the year from 1576, and from 1588 the gilt portrait-and-arms supralibros of the presentation bindings. Books received ready-bound, and gifts, may carry only his handwritten initials or a purchase-note. The periodisation is Prandtl’s; the numbering of the periods is this reconstruction’s own and is the scale used in the volume records.

PeriodDatesMarkIndicates
11560–1567Name blind-stamp ‘BRADE’ / ‘Tycho Brade’ + year; the two-line ‘TYCHO / BRAHE’ with 1567 on the Strahov Euclid (AV II 2)Student purchases; pre-Hven (Copenhagen, Leipzig, Rostock)
2c.1565–1575Gilt cipher T.B.O. (no date), brown calf, rhomboid arabesquePre-Hven acquisition
31576–1582T.B.O. 1576 (also 1580, 1582)Uraniborg-inauguration cohort; the Hven bindery
41588–1601Gilt supralibros portrait + arms (Prachtband)Presentation copies & select library books; earliest dated carrier the Royal Library's Sascerides De mundi (dedication 20 March 1588); the BL Maestlin copy, dispatched 14 May 1588, is the second
—throughoutHandwritten ‘T.B.’ initials or a purchase-noteGifts / ready-bound copies not stamped by the Hven bindery

Dated stamps recorded on the volumes catalogued here: T.B.O. 1576 (21); T.B.O. 1580 (1).

Recognition checklist

  • Upper-board oval gilt portrait medallion (two sizes: 7.6×5.8 cm or 5.8×4.3 cm) with the distich ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei…’ → Period-4 presentation Prachtband.
  • Lower-board arms oval with ‘Arma genus, fundi pereunt; durabile virtus…’.
  • Gilt T.B.O. / T.B.O. 1576 cipher on brown calf with a rhomboid arabesque → Period 2/3.
  • Handwritten ‘T.B.’ initials or a purchase-note on the title-page (gifts / ready-bound copies).
  • The Jesuit accession inscription ‘A. 1642 / Ex Bibliotheca Tychoniana’ (or Chomutov / Crusius) → Clementinum provenance.
  • Silk / satin / velvet binding with a hand-painted portrait → the highest gift tier.
  • A volume bearing only the Jesuit inscription, with no binding-stamp, is still Tycho's — Kleinschnitzová's explicit recovery route.

A caution. The Clementinum’s inscription Ex Bibliotheca Tychoniana is not by itself proof of Tycho’s ownership: the Jesuits went on adding to the Tychoniana after his death. Sign. 14 J 199, a Kepler imprint of 1606, carries the inscription and was printed five years after Tycho died; it is recorded here among the volumes marked Tychoniana but not his. Conversely, a volume bearing only the Jesuit inscription and no binding-stamp can still be Tycho’s: that is Kleinschnitzová’s explicit route of recovery.

8Acquisition and dispersal

How the books reached Tycho, and how they left his heirs. The acquisition channels are reconstructed from the correspondence and from the purchase-notes and dedications on the surviving copies. The dispersal channels are the routes by which the library scattered after 1601; each leaves its own diagnostic marks, which are the key to re-identifying his books in the collections where they now stand. Only the Clementinum channel is enumerated book by book; the others are documented as routes, and the count of entries assigned to each is given so that the limits of the enumeration are visible.

Acquisition channels

ChannelMechanismAgentsEntries assigned
Frankfurt book fairStanding orders via the biannual Willer catalogues, executed by correspondent-agents who scanned the fair and bought to order.Johannes Maior, Heinrich Brucaeus, Cunradus Aslachus, Herwart von Hohenburg10
Absorbed scholar-librariesThe systematic pursuit of a deceased mathematician's whole working library — mostly unsuccessful, but the most distinctive Tychonic method.Thaddaeus Hagecius, Jakob Monau, Longomontanus3
Author / correspondent giftPresentation copies delivered through the gift economy of the Republic of Letters.Heinrich Rantzau, Giordano Bruno, Johannes Kepler, Joseph Scaliger, Bartholomaeus Pitiscus, Thaddaeus Hagecius49
Manuscript copying & transmissionScribal copies made of texts he could not buy, and library-scouring missions (Vedel).Anders Sørensen Vedel, Thaddaeus Hagecius1
Direct / student purchaseBooks bought outright, often with an autograph purchase-note.3
Borrowed, not owned outside the cataloguesome fifty mathematical titles on loan from the Duke of Bavaria's library via Herwart in the Prague years — used but never owned, and so outside this catalogue.Herwart von Hohenburg0

Dispersal channels

ChannelNameMechanismDiagnostic marksPresent locationsExtentEntries assigned
IClementinum / Jesuit (1642 incorporation)Tycho's son-in-law Frans Gansneb Tengnagel — a Catholic convert who ran the posthumous editions — held the library together until his death in 1622, after which dispersal accelerated. In 1642 the heirs gave the surviving core, some twenty-three volumes, to the Jesuit Collegium Caesareum at the Clementinum in Prague, where the books were inscribed 'Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae A° 1642', usually with 'Ex Bibliotheca Tychoniana', and shelved as a separately-managed Musaeum Mathematicum (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 80-81). Further tranches reached the Jesuit colleges at Chomutov (Komotau) and Krumlov and the Professhaus on Prague's Malá Strana; the 1773 suppression of the Society and the secularisation of the monasteries re-converged those fragments in the Clementinum — which is why the mathematical and astronomical books are the part that survives. Gingerich's 2002 survey of the Clementinum volumes counts the marks as follows: sixteen carry the initials 'T.B.O.' tooled on the binding, six the gilt supralibros portrait, twelve the initials written in by hand, and two are author presentations (Bruno and Scaliger). Clear marginalia in Tycho's hand appear in only a few — among them the Ziegler In C. Plinii of 1531, in its Martianus Capella section, and Bartholomaeus Scultetus's Cometae of 1577.'Collegii Caesarei Soc. Jesu Pragae 1642' / 'Ex bibliotheca Tychoniana' inscription; the initials 'T.B.O.'/'T.B.O. 1576/1583' tooled on the binding; gilt supralibros portraitNational Library of the Czech Republic (Clementinum), Prague — the largest surviving fragment. Kleinschnitzová (1933) catalogued 97 works in 47 volumes; Šolc (2002) extends this to about 110 titles in some 50 volumes. This store itemises 87 Prague works in 53 volumes.53 volumes / 87 works itemised here93
IIHeirs' sale / dispersal (post-1601)After Tycho's death (1601) the family progressively sold off the library in Prague before bequeathing the remnant; this route probably took more of it than any other. How large the library was to begin with is itself disputed — estimates run from about 1,000 to about 3,000 volumes; the positions are set out under 'How big was the library?' below.later-owner inscriptions (e.g. Gabriel Crusius 1634/1673)scatterednot enumerated; probably the single largest route4
IIISwedish war-loot (1648 sack of Prague)The 1648 Swedish capture of Prague carried off Rudolfine/Bohemian holdings, including Tycho material, to Sweden and Denmark.Swedish royal/library provenanceUppsala; Stockholm; Copenhagensome volumes; not enumerated0
IVRudolfine-imperial absorptionSome volumes passed into the imperial/court orbit under Rudolf II.imperial provenanceVienna (ÖNB)some volumes; not enumerated2
VAttrition / lossWar, fire, and untraced dispersal account for the gap between the library as it stood at his death and the remnant located today — no single catastrophe, but a long attrition that left no mark to hunt by.the unrecovered remainder0
VIClementinum leakage → Strahov (Strnad and the Mathematical Museum surplus, after 1773)Two volumes carrying the 1642 inscription are now at Strahov, not in the Clementinum: Rheticus–Otho's Opus palatinum (Σ V 5/a) and the Regiomontanus Ephemerides (DR VII 19). The documented route out of the Clementinum is the one Boldan & Vackářová describe for the Mathematical Museum's library: after the suppression of 1773 Karel Rafael Ungar screened the incoming Jesuit and monastic books for duplicates, the observatory director Antonín Strnad bought part of the surplus astronomical volumes for himself, and from his estate they passed to Strahov, which bought the substantial part of his library after his death in 1799 (Munzar 2001). Straka gave exactly this chain for the Regiomontanus in 1913 — Clementinum → Strnad → Strahov — though Strahov's present cataloguer notes that the volume appears in neither published catalogue of Strnad's library (Seydl 1939; Kouklová 1989). The spine is the test: the Mathematical Museum's books carry no ex-libris, only red lines and an abbreviated title on the spine, and Strnad's books his handwritten name or name-stamp.the 1642 inscription on a book now outside the National Library; a Mathematical-Museum spine (red lines, abbreviated author/title); Antonín Strnad's name or stampStrahov Library, Prague — Σ V 5/a and DR VII 19 itemised here; the Strnad stratum at Strahov has never been sifted for further Tychoniana2 volumes itemised here2
VIIA private route that bypassed 1642 (the Strahov Euclid, via Clauser)Not every book of Tycho's went through the heirs' bequest. The Strahov Euclid of 1558 (AV II 2), stamped TYCHO BRAHE 1567 on its front board, carries no Jesuit inscription; its second recorded owner is Jan Josef Clauser (Klauser), the Prague printer and gubernial archivist whose library Strahov bought in 1775 (Neškudla 2021). The book therefore left Tycho's library — in Prague or earlier — by a private channel and reached the monastery through an eighteenth-century collector, the first confirmed instance of the pattern the orphan hunt was built to find: a Tycho-marked book lacking the Ex Bibliotheca Tychoniana leaf. Clauser's stratum at Strahov runs to some 2,850 records and has not been sifted for further Tycho marks.Tycho's own mark on the binding with no 1642 inscription; Clauser's printed ex-libris; an eighteenth-century Prague collector's provenanceStrahov Library, Prague — AV II 2 itemised here1 volume itemised here1

108 of the 210 entries carry no assigned dispersal channel: the book is attested as owned, but no documented route out of the heirs’ hands is recorded for it.

9Chronology

10Definitions and conventions

How an entry is to be read — its status, its two grades, its units — what each figure in this chapter counts, and what is known of the size of the library the figures describe.

How to read the entries

Status. Located: a physical copy identified as Tycho’s own survives and is recorded with its shelfmark. Attested, not located: a document names the book as Tycho’s, but no copy has been found; within this class, retired as unlocatable marks a mass-survival text whose copy would carry no known mark to search by. Disputed: ownership or identity is contested and the entry is kept out of the located count. Lost: a copy is recorded as destroyed, or as having vanished after being seen. Marked Tychoniana, not his: a volume that bears the Clementinum’s Tychoniana marks but was printed after Tycho’s death; it belongs to the history of the Jesuits’ Tychoniana, not to his library.

Grades. Two independent A–D scales are used. An entry’s confidence grades how securely the book can be asserted to have been Tycho’s: A, secure (a surviving copy with his marks, or an unambiguous document); B, probable; C, possible, resting on inference; D, doubtful. A surviving volume’s identification grades how securely that particular copy is his: A, his marks or hand on the copy itself; B, a catalogue or scholarly identification without a mark checked at first hand; C, circumstantial; D, doubtful. The grades are a deliverable of the reconstruction and are never rounded or removed.

Units. Entries count works, not volumes; a Sammelband holds several entries. Volumes count physical objects. No ratio of located to attested entries is a survival rate: a work enters the located tier because a copy was found, and most of that tier was compiled from the surviving Prague volumes in the first place. Of the whole library, estimated at between 1000 and 3000 volumes, the 71 located volumes represent roughly 2–7 per cent.

The size of the library

The library's original size is genuinely unresolved — estimates run from about 1,000 to about 3,000 volumes, and the headline figure rests on a single shelf-number.

EstimateProposed byBasis
about 3,000 volumesChristianson (2000)the lone shelf-number 2781 that Studnička found on a Gesner spine and Norlind reported
“at best speculative”Gingerich (2002)the 2781 appears in no other surviving volume; a 3,000-title library is plausible against Rantzau's 6,000 and Dee's about 4,000, but the number cannot bear the weight
about 1,000 volumes, about 2,000 worksMortensen (1955)the best-supported conservative figure
about 5,000 (rejected)Walde, via Mortensen 1942the outlier; Mortensen 1955 rejects it as physically impossible for the 5-metre museum room

Norlind himself wrote that “it is impossible to form any estimate of its size,” crediting the 2781 inference to Studnička.

11Desiderata

What remains to be found or resolved. 88 attested titles have no located copy: 54 carry a trace worth following (a title, an attestation, a last-known location), 32 are retired as unlocatable because the text survives in quantity and Tycho’s copy would carry no known mark to search by, and 2 are recorded as lost. The disputed identifications and the open questions attached to individual records follow. A scholar who can settle any of these is invited to write.

3(eight unidentified authors)Trace Mainx's eight Tycho books — which Prague monastery? Did Mainx publish them? The specific monastery's catalogue or Mainx's Nachlass is the next source.
3(eight unidentified authors): Strahov tested. Its only Tycho volume with autograph-attributed marginalia and a mark on the binding is the Euclid AV II 2, and its mark is a blind-stamped name and date of 1567 (Pařez 2009), not the gilt portrait plaque Mortensen ascribes to all eight; the Regiomontanus DR VII 19 has the 1642 inscription and no supralibros. Strahov's Tychoniana were surveyed by its own librarian in 1996 and 2009 and its bindings by Straka (1919, 1920), Hamanová–Nuska (1966) and Voit (2020). On Mortensen's description Strahov is not Mainx's monastery; the question stays open for Emauzy, Břevnov and the others.

12History of the library

An account of the library from 1560 to the identification of its surviving volumes, drawn from the sources listed in the final section. It is given for orientation; every specific claim in the catalogue rests on the source cited in its own record.

Formation of the library, 1560–1597

On 21 August 1560 Tycho, then a thirteen-year-old student at Copenhagen, observed a partial solar eclipse that had been predicted. Gassendi, in Dreyer's rendering, says that it struck him “as something divine that men could know the motions of the stars so accurately that they could long before foretell their places and relative positions”, and that he procured the Ephemerides of Stadius. The Ptolemy in Prague (Omnia quae extant opera, Basel 1551; NK ČR 5 B 70) carries at the foot of its title page the note Emptus Haffniae 2 Joachimicis 1560 ultimo Novembris: bought at Copenhagen for two Joachimsthaler on 30 November 1560. Dreyer, following Friis, read the note as Tycho's hand and made this the first book of the library. The same title page carries the name of Johannes Pratensis (1543–1576), Tycho's friend and later professor of medicine, and the binding is stamped with his initials and the year 1561. Studnička (1901) took Pratensis for the seller; Boldan and Vackářová (2024) take him for the first owner and suppose that the book passed to Tycho from his estate. The hand of the note has not been examined, and the question is open. That the copy was Tycho's is not in doubt: it carries marginal notes which an early note on the title page assigns to him (Marginales notae sunt Tichonis Brahe), and the Jesuit inscription of 1642. From 1562 Tycho studied at Leipzig, where he bought astronomical books without the knowledge of his tutor (Dreyer). The earliest dated marks of ownership are name-stamps of 1561, 1563 and 1567 (Norlind; Pařez 2009). A large group of the surviving volumes is stamped T.B.O. 1576, the year Frederik II granted him Hven (Norlind).

The library at Uraniborg

The library occupied the southern round room on the ground floor of Uraniborg. In the plan Tycho printed in the Mechanica it is T, Bibliotheca; W is the great brass globe and V the four tables for the students. The globe, almost six Tychonic feet (about 149 cm) in diameter, stood in the middle of the room, and portraits of Hipparchus, Ptolemy and al-Battani hung on the walls (Christianson). The chemical laboratory lay in the basement beneath the room, the southern observatory above it. Beside the printing office Tycho set up a bindery, and from 1592 a paper mill, on the island (Nielsen; Vellev). The bindery bound not only his own publications but the books he acquired for the library, and stamped them with his marks (Prandtl); this is why so many of his books can be recognised today.

Acquisition

Tycho's correspondents were also his suppliers (Mosley). He bought at the Frankfurt fairs through the printed fair catalogues and through agents who bought to order: Johannes Maior, Heinrich Brucaeus at Rostock, Cunradus Aslachus and, in the Prague years, Herwart von Hohenburg, the Bavarian chancellor. He repeatedly tried to acquire the whole working library of a dead mathematician. The attempts on the books of Ambrose of Augsburg (1575), Brechtalius (1576) and Dudith (about 1600) failed; the papers of Rheticus were sought from Hagecius in 1592 and those of Leovitius through the Fugger library; the pursuit of Wittich's library, in three attempts between 1589 and 1598, brought his annotated copies of De revolutionibus to Prague in October 1600 (Mosley; Gingerich). Presentation copies came from authors and correspondents, among them Rantzau, Bruno, Kepler, Scaliger and Pitiscus. In the Prague years part of the working library was borrowed: from a catalogue of the Bavarian ducal library's mathematical books, obtained through Herwart, Tycho selected fifty, which Herwart sent him in batches on loan (Mosley). These are outside the catalogue, since he never owned them.

The ownership marks

Four periods of binding marks can be distinguished (Prandtl; Kleinschnitzová; Mortensen 1931). Period 1, 1560–1567: a stamped name and year on the front board — Tycho Brade 1561, Ty Brad 1563, and TYCHO / BRAHE 1567 on the Strahov Euclid. Period 2, about 1565–1575: brown calf with the gilt initials T.B.O. (Tycho Brahe, son of Otte), undated. Period 3, 1576–1582: the same initials with a year, T.B.O. 1576, also 1580 and 1582, the bindings of the first Uraniborg years. Period 4, 1588–1601: the gilt portrait supralibros, an oval medallion of Tycho in a ruff, wearing on chains the Frederik II medallion and an elephant pendant, on the upper board, and his arms on the lower, each ringed by a distich. It exists in two sizes, and the earliest dated binding to carry it is the Royal Library's Sascerides copy of De mundi, with Tycho's dedication of 20 March 1588. Books bought ready-bound or received as gifts may carry only the handwritten initials T.B. or a purchase note; the absence of a stamp does not exclude Tycho's ownership.

Exile and death, 1597–1601

Tycho's pension was stopped on 18 March 1597. On 21 March his assistants catalogued all the books on Hven (the meteorological diary; TBOO IX, 146), and on 29 March he left the island. The library went with him: to Copenhagen, on 2 June into exile at Rostock, to Wandsbek as Rantzau's guest, to Wittenberg for the winter of 1598–99, and in 1599 into the service of Rudolf II in Bohemia, where books and instruments were together again at Prague in 1600. Tycho died at Prague on 24 October 1601. His heirs sold the instruments and the observation books to the Emperor for 20,000 thalers, of which 4,000 had been paid by 1603; the balance was never paid (Dreyer; Kleinschnitzová). The observation books, lent to Kepler, were sold by his son Ludwig to Frederik III of Denmark in 1655 and are in Copenhagen (Mortensen). The library itself was not bought. It stayed with the heirs, impoverished by the unpaid debt and several of them converts to Catholicism, and was sold and given away piecemeal over the following decades.

The Clementinum and the sack of 1648

Tycho's son-in-law Frans Gansneb Tengnagel, who intended to continue the work, died in 1622, and the dispersal quickened: a book from the library was in private hands at Budějovice by 1623 (Kleinschnitzová). In 1642 the Jesuit college in the Clementinum received a group of volumes from the heirs — Kleinschnitzová counts twenty-three — and inscribed each title page Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae A. 1642, usually with Ex Bibliotheca Tychoniana; they were kept in the college's Mathematical Museum. Other volumes reached the Jesuit colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov, the Jesuit professed house in the Malá Strana, and private owners; after the suppression of the Society in 1773 these parts were brought together in the Clementinum, which is why the National Library of the Czech Republic holds the largest surviving portion of the library. In July 1648 the Swedish general Königsmarck took Hradčany and the Malá Strana, on the west bank of the Vltava, and the Rudolfine collections in the Castle were carried off to Sweden. Gingerich traces one of Wittich's annotated copies of De revolutionibus, acquired by Tycho in 1600, from Rudolf's collection through the Swedish booty and Queen Christina's library to the Vatican (Ott. lat. 1902). The Clementinum stands in the Old Town on the east bank, which the Swedes did not take; the volumes of 1642 were untouched.

Strahov: the second Prague site

The Strahov Library, the Premonstratensian house on the hill above Pohořelec, where Tycho died, holds five volumes from his library and two that he gave away; none of them had entered this reconstruction before September 2026. Four carry his marks on the binding (Pařez 2009). The Euclid of Basel 1558 in the Zamberti–Campanus translation (AV II 2) has TYCHO / BRAHE and the year 1567 blind-stamped on the front board, the only dated name-stamp in the spelling Brahe (those of 1561 and 1563 read Brade and Brad); it dates from the Rostock years, and its marginal notes, which Pařez attributes to Tycho, have not been transcribed or reproduced. Rheticus and Otho's Opus palatinum of 1596 (Σ V 5/a) and Ramus's Arithmeticae libri duo of 1580 (AG XIV 7) are bound in parchment with the full-size gilt portrait and arms plaques; the binding of the former is attributed to a Prague workshop of the Rudolfine circle and dated 1599–1601 (Voit 2020). A convolute of Olympia Morata, Fungerus and Gwalther (Σ VI 3), in leather, carries the smaller plaques. The fifth volume, a Regiomontanus (DR VII 19), has no supralibros. It consists of the Augsburg almanac of 1492 preceded by the prefatory gatherings of the Venice Ephemerides of 1481, both from Ratdolt's press, and carries the Jesuit inscription of 1642 and, on the verso of the leaf for December 1495, a Latin note of thirty-four lines on the winter of 1495/96. Cyrill Straka published the note in 1913 and attributed it to Tycho's hand on a comparison he did not document; Munzar and Pařez (2002) supported the attribution from the content, Boldan (2025) repeats it, and it has not been tested against the secure specimens of the hand. Boldan also shows that this volume and the National Library's Ephemerides of 1481 (Kleinschnitzová 14) are two parts of one book: the Strahov volume has the prefatory gatherings the Clementinum copy lacks.

The volumes reached Strahov by at least three routes. The Opus palatinum and the Regiomontanus carry the 1642 inscription, so both were in the Clementinum and later left it. Boldan and Vackářová document a route out: after 1773 Karel Rafael Ungar screened the incoming Jesuit books for duplicates, much of the Mathematical Museum's library was discarded, Antonín Strnad, director of the Clementinum observatory, bought the surplus astronomical volumes, and Strahov bought the greater part of his library after his death in 1799. Straka gave this chain for the Regiomontanus in 1913, but the volume appears in neither published catalogue of Strnad's books, and Strahov's own cataloguer suspects a confusion with another almanac from Strnad's library; for the Opus palatinum no route beyond the inscription is recorded. The Euclid has no Jesuit mark. Its next recorded owner is Jan Josef Clauser, the Prague printer and gubernial archivist, whose library the monastery bought in 1775 (Neškudla 2021); it reached Strahov without passing through the Clementinum, and when it left Tycho's library is not known. The two presentation copies were never part of his library: the Mechanica in green silk with a bound-in watercolour portrait (AG XI 56), and the Progymnasmata with a full-length watercolour, of which Šafařík distributed photolithographs in 1881 and which has not been traced since. Both were Tycho's gifts to Jan Zbyněk Zajíc z Házmburka (c. 1570–1616), and how Házmburk's books came to Strahov is undocumented. None of the three strata — Strnad's, Clauser's and Házmburk's — has been searched for further volumes with Tycho's marks.

The identification of the surviving volumes, 1868–2026

The surviving volumes have been identified in a sequence of studies. Friis (1868) surveyed the Tychonic manuscripts in Vienna and Prague. Studnička (1901) described the Prague Tychoniana, among them the Ptolemy of 1551 and the annotated De revolutionibus of 1566. Dreyer's edition of the Opera omnia (1913–29) printed the correspondence in which many of the books are named. Prandtl (1932) catalogued the surviving volumes by author and by volume; his Band numbers are used in the concordance here. Kleinschnitzová (1933) catalogued the 97 works in 47 volumes then identified in the Clementinum, with the history of the dispersal. Mortensen (1955) added the volumes in Denmark and elsewhere outside Prague, among them the Copenhagen Calvin–Theocritus volume with Tycho's dedication to Hans Lindenov. Norlind (1970) reconstructed a catalogue of some 216 titles from the surviving volumes and from the books named in Tycho's writings and letters. Šolc (2002) recounted the Clementinum holding at about 110 titles in 50 volumes, and Gingerich (2002) located dispersed volumes in Texas, Chicago and the Vatican. Pařez (2009) published the Strahov supralibros and Boldan (2025) the Strahov Regiomontanus. This reconstruction is built on that work.

The volume of 1561: Munich, America, Helsingør

Prandtl’s Band II — Regiomontanus’s Tabulae directionum (Tübingen 1550) bound with Apianus’s Cosmographia in Gemma Frisius’s recension (Paris 1553), in brown calf stamped TYCHO BRADE on the front board and ANNO 1561 on the back, with the purchase note ‘emptus thalero & 4 Gross’ and Tycho’s name three times on the pastedown — is one of the student bindings. Prandtl saw it at Antiquariat Weiss & Co. in Munich and recorded in 1932 that it had been sold to America; Gingerich (2002) still placed it at an undisclosed location, and this reconstruction carried it as a private, untraced volume until September 2026. It had in fact returned to Denmark within a generation. The Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg reported it among the acquisitions of 1956–57 as the gift of Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman, and Norlind’s catalogue of 1970 placed it there — a location transcribed under both entries here but not carried into the volume record until now. The museum’s register (inventory number 1957:0030) describes the binding, the inscriptions, Tycho’s added latitudes for Helsingborg, Lund and Visby on fol. 53 of the Apianus, and a restoration by Birgitte Dall in 1957; two photographs on the public record show the front board and the purchase note. Björklund reported in 1992 that the volume, with Latin plant names written at the head of its pages in another hand and plant fragments still between the leaves, had been deposited by the museum at the Royal Library’s manuscript department, and the Nationalmuseet’s catalogue of 2006 reproduced it from a Royal Library photograph. The museum, now M/S Museet for Søfart at Helsingør, files the record under its deposits. Whether the volume is in the Royal Library or has returned to the museum’s store has not been confirmed.

The two tiers of the catalogue are built in opposite directions: the located tier from the surviving volumes to the entries they prove, the attested tier from documents to books that have not been found.

    Tycho Brahe, Epistolae: the 509 letters of J. L. E. Dreyer’s Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, vols VI–VIII (Copenhagen, 1919–1925), served as a digital edition by Det Danske Sprog- og Litteraturselskab, ed. Peter Zeeberg (tekstnet.dk).
    Contributes The acquisition record by proxy: books requested, sent, given, lent or discussed in the letters. Each letter-attested entry links to the letter.
    Open copy tekstnet.dk
  16. NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph)

    Contributes The record-level catalogue links and the verbatim copy-level provenance notes quoted under the Prague volumes.
    Open copy aleph.nkp.cz
  17. Manuscriptorium

Records CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Harvested 9 September 2026 through the library's catalogue and OAI-PMH interfaces.
    Contributes The catalogue-record fields, binding descriptions, former-owner entries, provenance notes and facsimiles quoted under the Prague volumes.
    Open copy Manuscriptorium
  18. Supralibros note
    ‘Tycho Brahe’s Gilt-Stamped Supralibros Portrait: Earliest Uses and Origins’ — an unpublished research note on the earliest dated uses of the portrait stamp and the engraving it derives from.
    Contributes Used at one entry, to date the portrait stamp.
  19. Žemla 2025

    Contributes Checking which Hagecius edition is which.
  20. Schrimpf & Verbunt 2021
    Andreas Schrimpf and Frank Verbunt, ‘The star catalogue of Wilhelm IV, Landgraf von Hessen-Kassel’, in G. Wolfschmidt (ed.), Applied and computational historical astronomy (Nuncius Hamburgensis 55, 2021); arXiv:2103.10801.
    Contributes Context for the Kassel observation material in the letters.

  21. WorldCat
    OCLC WorldCat, the union catalogue of library holdings.
    Contributes Checking imprints and titles; nothing else.
    Open copy search.worldcat.org
  22. Pařez 2009
    Jan Pařez, ‘Supralibros dánského astronoma Tycha Brahe ve Strahovské knihovně’, Sborník pro exlibris a drobnou grafiku 2009 (Spolek sběratelů a přátel exlibris, Praha), pp. 24–26, with photographs of the Euclid’s 1567 name-stamp and of the portrait and arms supralibros on Σ V 5 and Σ VI 3. The only description of the four Strahov volumes from Tycho’s library together; credits the discovery of the Euclid to Hedvika Kuchařová.
    Contributes The Strahov supralibros; the basis of the four Strahov entries.
    Open copy Spolek sběratelů a přátel exlibris — the whole Sborník as a PDF
  23. Straka 1913
    Cyrill Straka, ‘Zápis Tychona Brahe v knihovně Strahovské’, Časopis Musea království Českého 87 (1913), pp. 382–384. The discovery note on the Strahov Regiomontanus: the two Ratdolt incunables, the 1642 inscription, the 34-line weather note (Latin text in part, Czech paraphrase), the later owners Nachlovský and Worell, and the chain Clementinum → Strnad → Strahov.
    Contributes First publication of the Strahov Regiomontanus and of the attribution of its note to Tycho.
    Open copy NK ČR Kramerius — p. 382
  24. Boldan 2025
    Kamil Boldan, ‘Ratdoltova astronomika v českých a moravských knihovnách’, Knihy a dějiny 32 (2025), no. 1–2, pp. 9–41 (DOI 10.23852/KAD.2025.32.01). A census of 104 Ratdolt astronomica in Czech libraries; entries 33.b, 33.c and 36.a describe the National Library’s Venice 1481 Ephemerides (40 F 39, Tycho’s, lacking its first gatherings) and the Strahov volume DR VII 19 (the Augsburg 1492 Ephemerides with the 1481 prefatory gatherings bound before it, the weather note at fol. e4v).
    Contributes The modern description of DR VII 19; establishes that the Strahov and National Library Regiomontanus volumes are two halves of one book.
    Open copy Knihy a dějiny — open access, the DOI opens the PDF
  25. Kroupa 2001
    Jiří K. Kroupa, ‘První vydání díla Tychona Brahe Astronomiae instauratae mechanica v českých knihovnách’, Bulletin plus (Národní knihovna ČR) 4/2001. The three Bohemian copies of the 1598 Mechanica compared (Strahov AG XI 56, Křivoklát III-a-18, NK ČR 14 A 291) with the three Paris copies; the Strahov copy’s green silk binding, dedication text and bound-in watercolour.
    Contributes The Strahov Mechanica’s binding and watercolour; the Křivoklát copy’s route through the Clementinum.
    Open copy Wayback Machine — the Bulletin plus page as it stood in 2012

    Contributes The holding library’s own provenance record for each copy.
    Open copy strahovskyklaster.tritius.cz

    Contributes The binder attribution of the Opus palatinum.
    Open copy nusk.upce.cz

    Petr Voit, Vzácné knižní vazby Strahovské knihovny v Praze: od gotiky na práh baroka (Bibliotheca Strahoviensis, Series monographica IX; Praha 2020), pp. 250–252 — the Opus palatinum binding and the group of presentation bindings made for Tycho.
    Contributes The published description of the Opus palatinum binding; not read at first hand.
  29. Pařez 1996
    Jan Pařez, ‘Tychoniana ve Strahovské knihovně’, Příspěvky ke Knihopisu 11 (Praha 1996), pp. 89–95. The survey of all Strahov Tychoniana, written before the Euclid was found.
    Contributes Nothing yet — the earlier Strahov survey, not read.
    Open copy NK ČR Kramerius — digitised, access-restricted
  30. Munzar & Pařez 2002
    Jan Munzar & Jan Pařez, ‘Tycho Brahe as a Meteorologist’, in J. R. Christianson, A. Hadravová, P. Hadrava and M. Šolc (eds), Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science (Acta Historica Astronomiae 16; Frankfurt am Main: Harri Deutsch, 2002), pp. 360–375 — the transcription, translation and dating of the winter-1495/96 note in the Strahov Regiomontanus (pp. 369–374), with a letter-by-letter comparison of its hand against the DG IV 25 motto and the AG XI 56 dedication.
    Contributes The argument that the note is Tycho’s: the hand ‘with a high probability’ his, and at the least a person of his immediate circle; the winter 1495/96 rather than 1595/96, from independent climate records, a reconstruction of the planetary positions at the 1495 solstice and the chronology of the venereal epidemic; the note read as a retrospective astrometeorological reconstruction, not a Bohemian weather record.
  31. Neškudla 2021
    Bořek Neškudla, ‘Přehled dosavadního bádání o knihovnách premonstrátských klášterů’, Bibliotheca Strahoviensis 14 (2021), pp. 227–244, at p. 229: Strahov bought the library of the Prague printer and gubernial archivist Jan Josef Klauser in 1775, Heidel’s in 1780, Riegger’s in 1794, and absorbed the Norbertinum’s in 1787.
    Contributes The date the Clauser books reached Strahov.
    Open copy Strahov Library — Bibliotheca Strahoviensis 14 (PDF, 5 MB)

    Jan Munzar, ‘200. výročí úmrtí astronoma Antonína Strnada (1746–1799)’, Bibliotheca Strahoviensis 4–5 (2001), pp. 269–271: Strahov bought the substantial part of Strnad’s library after his death; the three studies of it are Seydl 1939, Kouklová 1985/86 and Kouklová 1989.
    Contributes The route by which Strnad’s books reached Strahov.
    Open copy Strahov Library — Bibliotheca Strahoviensis 4–5 (PDF, 166 MB)

    František Josef Studnička, Prager Tychoniana (Prague, 1901). The Tycho relics in Prague as seen in 1901, among them the Ptolemy of 1551 (the purchase note read as Tycho’s hand, Pratensis taken for the seller, p. 39) and the annotated De revolutionibus of 1566.
    Contributes The Prague holdings before Prandtl and Kleinschnitzová; the first reading of the Ptolemy’s title page.
    Open copy NK ČR Kramerius — digitised, public
  34. Boldan & Vackářová 2024
    Kamil Boldan & Jana Vackářová, Bibliotheca astronomica. Astronomické tisky 15.–17. století ze sbírek Národní knihovny ČR (Prague: Národní knihovna ČR, 2024), pp. 88–101 (Tycho’s library and its marks) and 141–144 (the later fortunes of the books: Ungar’s duplicate screening after 1773, Strnad’s purchases, and the Ptolemy 5 B 70 read with Johannes Pratensis as first owner).
    Contributes The National Library’s own reading of its Tycho volumes and of the eighteenth-century routes out of the Clementinum.
    Open copy Národní knihovna ČR — the catalogue as a PDF, at p. 88
  35. Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957
    Knud Klem, ‘Museets komité og beretning om regnskabsåret 1956–57’, Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg: Årbog 1957 (Helsingør: Selskabet Handels- og Søfartsmuseets Venner, 1957), pp. 1–21. The museum’s report for the year records, among the acquisitions of 1956–57, Regiomontanus’s Tabulae directionum (1550) bound with Apianus’s Cosmographia (1553) in a contemporary binding, ‘which belonged to Tycho Brahe’, as the gift of Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman, with Tycho’s own note that he bought it in 1561 for one thaler and four groschen.
    Contributes The acquisition record of Prandtl’s Band II, the student binding of 1561.
    Open copy tidsskrift.dk
  36. Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart)
    Slots- og Kulturstyrelsen, Museernes Samlinger: the object record of M/S Museet for Søfart, inventory number 1957:0030, ‘Astronomi (bog fra Tycho Brahes bibliotek)’ — the museum’s description of the two works, the binding with its stamps TVCHO BRADE and ANNO 1561, the ownership inscriptions and the purchase note, Tycho’s added latitudes for Helsingborg, Lund and Visby on fol. 53 of the Apianus, and the restoration of 1957, with two photographs (the front board; the pastedown with the purchase note beside the Regiomontanus title).
    Contributes The holding museum’s own record and photographs of Band II.
    Open copy samlinger.slks.dk
  37. Björklund 1992
    Per-Åke Björklund, Tycho Brahe og Kamarillaen (Copenhagen: Rhodos, 1992), p. 26: the Regiomontanus of 1561, lately come to light at the Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg, ‘now deposited at the Royal Library’s manuscript department’; Latin plant names written at the head of the pages in another hand, and plant fragments still between the leaves — the volume had served as a herbarium.
    Contributes The deposit of Band II at the Royal Library, and its use as a herbarium.
  38. Grinder-Hansen 2006
    Poul Grinder-Hansen (ed.), Tycho Brahes Verden: Danmark i Europa 1550–1600 (Copenhagen: Nationalmuseet, 2006), p. 49, fig. 5: the volume of 1561 reproduced — ‘Bogen tilhører Handels- og Søfartsmuseet. Det Kongelige Bibliotek foto.’
    Contributes The 2006 reproduction of Band II, photographed at the Royal Library.

The Clementinum count

Kleinschnitzová (1933) records 97 works in 47 volumes; Šolc (2002) extends this to about 110 titles in some 50 volumes. This reconstruction itemises 88 works in 51 National Library volumes: more volumes than either earlier count, fewer works. Part of the difference is a matter of grain: constituents Šolc counts separately are here folded into their parent works (the Regiomontanus oration and the Melanchthon epistle that are front-matter of the Alfraganus, and two cometary tracts inside the comet Sammelband). The residual difference of about 18 titles is stated rather than closed: not every work Šolc counts has yet been itemised here.

How to cite this chapter. Bibliotheca Tychoniana — The Library of Tycho Brahe, Tychoniana, version of 5 September 2026, accessed . Cite an entry by its record key, e.g. “no. 1, record e-mort-tuwien-alphonsine”. The complete dataset behind the page is published beside it as data.json; the catalogue table can be exported as CSV from section 2. A summary report is at index.html.
